sources.cite: AWS IAM User Guide, 'AWS: Denies access to AWS based on the requested Region'
sources.note: Read through a summarizing fetch on 2026-11-17. Quoted: 'Actions in the CloudFront, IAM, Route 53, and Support services should not be denied because these are popular AWS global services with a single endpoint that is physically located in the us-east-1 Region ... the requests would be denied without the NotAction element'; the example's NotAction lists cloudfront, iam, organizations, route53 and support, and the page says to extend it for other global services you use (budgets, globalaccelerator, waf ...). The page covers identity policies; that the same pattern is used in an SCP, that an SCP grants nothing and an explicit deny in an SCP overrides any allow in the account, and the CloudTrail message wording are from memory of the AWS Organizations guide (to verify).

brief.situation: You are the cloud architect at Verity Health Analytics, a fictional company whose customer data must stay in the EU. This morning the platform team attached a new SCP, eu-only, to the Workloads OU: it denies every action whose requested Region is not eu-central-1 or eu-west-1. Since then every deployment in Workloads fails. The product launch deploys at 16:00.
handover: The launch stack creates an IAM role, updates a CloudFront distribution and adds Route 53 records.
The compliance officer signed off the eu-only guardrail; it must stay in force for the regulated accounts.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the organization's OUs, the eu-only SCP and the calls the deployment makes.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The launch deploys at 16:00; the stack needs about 5 minutes after the policy is fixed.

effects.finding: The deny covers every action. Global services such as IAM, CloudFront and Route 53 have one endpoint in us-east-1, so their calls are always 'outside' the allowed Regions.

exempt.label: Update eu-only to Deny with NotAction for the global services the workloads use, test in the sandbox OU, then update the Workloads policy
exempt.available: not busy and (not fixed and not harmed)
exempt.why: Already done, or the system is down.

effects.output:
arch@mgmt:~$ aws organizations update-policy --policy-id p-euonly-test --content file://eu-only-v2.json   # NotAction: iam, organizations, route53, cloudfront, support, waf, budgets, sts
arch@mgmt:~$ ./scp-probe --ou sandbox  # iam:CreateRole OK; ec2:RunInstances us-east-1 DENIED; ec2:RunInstances eu-central-1 OK
arch@mgmt:~$ aws organizations update-policy --policy-id p-euonly --content file://eu-only-v2.json

effects.log: Calls to global services pass; any regional action outside the two EU Regions is still denied, which is what the residency rule needs. The test OU showed both before the change reached Workloads.

writeup.question: For the record: why the deployments failed, how you fixed it without losing the residency control, and how the next SCP change is tested.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: Connects the explicit deny to global endpoints.
parts.modelAnswer: CloudTrail showed explicit denies from an SCP on IAM, CloudFront and Route 53. eu-only denied every action whose requested Region was not in the EU, and those global services have a single endpoint in us-east-1.

parts.label: Fix
parts.criteria: Narrows the deny and keeps the control.
parts.modelAnswer: eu-only v2 denies with NotAction for the global services we use, so regional actions outside the EU are still denied. Tested in the sandbox OU first. Detaching it would have removed a signed-off residency control; AdministratorAccess cannot override an SCP deny.

parts.label: Next time
parts.modelAnswer: The exemption list is reviewed with compliance, and the policy pipeline runs a probe in the sandbox OU before any SCP reaches Workloads.

expertPath.text: CloudTrail: explicit SCP deny on IAM, CloudFront, Route 53; eu-only denies all actions; attached to Workloads; the role allows the calls.
eu-only v2 with NotAction for global services, tested in sandbox, applied; sign-off and an SCP test in the pipeline.
Change set completes; us-east-1 EC2 still denied.

guardrailRemoved.headline: The control was right; its scope was wrong
guardrailRemoved.body: The deny was meant for regional actions. Exempting global services keeps the residency rule and lets the deployment work; removing it breaks a signed-off compliance control.

launchSlipped.headline: No IAM allow beats an SCP deny
launchSlipped.body: An SCP sets the maximum for every principal in the account. Fix the SCP (NotAction for global services); permissions inside the account cannot override it.

scoped.headline: Good: guardrail kept, scope corrected
scoped.body: You read the deny in CloudTrail, saw the policy covered global services with us-east-1 endpoints, tested an exemption list in a sandbox OU, kept the residency rule, and put an SCP test in the pipeline.

gaps.headline: Held, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria show what was left: the evidence before the change, the lasting step, the check, or the cause in the record.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: The failures are explicit denies from an SCP, all on global services whose single endpoint is in us-east-1, so a Region deny on every action blocks them. Keep the residency rule and narrow it: deny with NotAction for the global services the workloads use, test it in a sandbox OU, then apply it. Detaching the SCP removes a compliance control; no IAM allow can override an SCP deny. Then review the exemptions with compliance and test SCP changes before they reach production OUs.
